title: HSBC's Restructuring Strategy Delivers Results: Is More Upside Ahead?

HSBC's Restructuring Strategy Delivers Results: Is More Upside Ahead?

HSBC Holdings plc HSBC is advancing its organizational restructuring strategy to simplify operations, reduce structural costs and concentrate resources on businesses and markets with stronger growth potential. The strategy is beginning to deliver benefits, with cost reductions from organizational simplification partly offsetting inflation and higher planned technology investments.

HSBC's third-quarter 2026 performance reflects improving operational efficiency, supported by disciplined expense management and business simplification. With restructuring initiatives gaining traction, the key question is whether these efficiency improvements can support sustainable earnings growth.

HSBC's Strategic Overhaul and Cost Initiatives Drive Efficiency

HSBC's restructuring strategy centers on simplifying its global operations and directing resources toward businesses offering stronger growth and returns. The company reorganized its operations into four businesses — Hong Kong, UK, Corporate and Institutional Banking, and International Wealth and Premier Banking.

This streamlined structure aims to reduce management layers, eliminate operational redundancies and improve decision-making efficiency. HSBC has also been optimizing its business portfolio through selective divestments and exits from non-core markets. The strategy includes exiting selected non-core operations and consolidating parts of its international footprint. HSBC plans to wind down its German transaction-services business, with approximately 320 positions expected to be phased out by 2028, following earlier exits from private banking and custody-related activities in Germany. These transactions align with HSBC's broader effort to focus on businesses where it sees stronger long-term growth and returns.

Cost optimization remains another important pillar of the transformation. By the first half of 2026, HSBC had completed actions expected to generate $1.7 billion in annualized savings. The bank remains on track to generate $2 billion in annualized organizational simplification savings by the end of 2026. These savings are expected to lower its structural cost base and create additional capacity for investment in priority businesses.

These initiatives should gradually lower HSBC's structural cost base, improve operating leverage and enhance capital efficiency. However, targeted annualized savings should not be confused with cost reductions fully realized during 2026.

Investing.com -- Citi told clients in a new note that short positioning in U.S. small caps remains near historical extremes, increasing the risk of a short squeeze if a catalyst emerges.

The bank said global positioning activity turned bearish across the board last week, after a rotation into Europe the week before. Investors de-risked across equity indices, largely by initiating new short positions.

Citi added that in the U.S., investors continued to cut growth exposure and add shorts. Nasdaq positioning has decreased significantly over the past two weeks but remains net long, while Russell 2000 positioning remains pinned at the bottom of its historical distribution, though activity there was muted last week.

"Elevated profitability among Russell shorts increases vulnerability to any catalyst capable of initiating forced cover activity," Citi wrote.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

In Europe, the previous week's broad-based inflows reversed. Fresh longs in the FTSE 100 were covered, pushing positioning net negative, while shorts were added in the DAX and Euro Stoxx. Citi noted that French fiscal concerns persist and that bearish positions in European banks increased.

Asia is said to remain the weakest region globally, with short activity having increased further in the Hang Seng and KOSPI, even though both are at or near maximum normalized bearish positioning.

Citi said the absence of meaningful long participation suggests bearish sentiment has yet to stabilize. Much of the short base in both markets is sitting profitably in the money.

"While positioning momentum remains decisively negative, increasingly crowded short exposure raises the risk of an outsized short-covering response should sentiment improve," the bank said.

title: BOH Expands Buyback Plan: Can It Sustain Strong Capital Returns?

Trading disclosure

Bank of Hawaii Corporation BOH reinforced its commitment to shareholder returns by expanding its share repurchase authorization by $200 million, bringing the remaining buyback capacity to $268.7 million. Following $20.2 million in repurchases during the third quarter of 2026, management plans another $20 million in buybacks in the fourth quarter. The expanded authorization provides flexibility to accelerate capital distributions, depending on earnings performance and capital requirements.

The decision comes amid improving profitability. Third-quarter net income increased 20.5% year over year to $64.3 million, while earnings per share rose to $1.49 from $1.20. Net interest income increased 14.2% to $156.1 million, supported by a four-basis-point sequential improvement in the net interest margin (NIM) to 2.82%. Notably, margin expansion continued for the tenth consecutive quarter, reflecting higher asset yields and disciplined deposit pricing

BOH's Solid Capital and Liquidity Aid Shareholder Returns

Bank of Hawaii maintains a strong capital position, supporting continued shareholder distributions. Its Tier 1 capital ratio stood at 14.41% at September-end, comfortably above regulatory requirements, while the Tier 1 leverage ratio improved to 8.79% from 8.57% at 2025-end. The company also maintained its quarterly common dividend at 70 cents per share, equivalent to $2.80 annually. It has a dividend yield of 4.3%.

BOH's liquidity position remains resilient. At September-end, the company held $442 million in cash and cash equivalents, and $3.5 billion in available-for-sale securities. These liquidity sources provide financial flexibility to meet funding requirements while supporting capital returns.

Earnings prospects also remain encouraging, with the Zacks Consensus Estimate for BOH's 2026 earnings pointing to 27% year-over-year growth. Expected earnings improvement, coupled with solid capitalization and ample liquidity, could further strengthen the company's capacity to generate shareholder value.

Overall, BOH's expanded share repurchase program underscores management's confidence in the company's financial position and earnings outlook. Strong capital adequacy, resilient liquidity and anticipated earnings growth provide support for continued capital returns. However, maintaining a prudent balance between shareholder distributions, balance-sheet resilience and growth opportunities will remain essential.

The third-quarter 2026 earnings season is in full swing now. Most of the major investment banks have reported their quarterly financial numbers. Here, we recommend two giant investment banks to buy for various reasons.

The Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

Goldman Sachs benefited from strong revenue growth in the Global Banking & Markets and Asset & Wealth Management businesses. Improving deal activity and robust equity trading of GS should support fee-income growth.
